extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Pascal, theology, Christian apologetics, and readers of classic French philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of normative and evaluative principles appearing in an annotated edition of Pascal's Pensées (aphoristic fragments and editorial notes). The page contains short aphorisms that function as theological, moral, and rhetorical standards or critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and plurality
rubrics_metrics.description: Duo aut tres in unum. Unity and plurality. It is an error to exclude one of the two, as the papists do who exclude plurality, or the Huguenots who exclude unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a balance between unity and plurality; avoiding the error of denying either pole (neither exclude plurality nor exclude unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infallibility more plausible in a multitude than in one man
rubrics_metrics.description: God does not perform miracles in the ordinary conduct of His Church. It would be a strange miracle if infallibility existed in one man. But it appears so natural for it to reside in a multitude...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal argues infallibility is more credible when located in the collective (multitude) than concentrated in a single individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on papal disposal of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Kings dispose of their own power; but the Popes cannot dispose of theirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes temporal sovereigns from ecclesiastical office: papal power has constraints that kings' power does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority, might, and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Summum jus, summa injuria. The majority is the best way, because it is visible, and has strength to make itself obeyed. Yet it is the opinion of the least able... they have placed justice in the hands of might.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that majority rule often equates what is obeyed with what is 'just'—a caution about conflating power with justice (the 'right of the sword').

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction is not given for the sake of the judge, but for that of the litigant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictional authority should serve the litigant's interests; be cautious in explaining this to the populace, but recognize it as the proper end of judicial power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular desire for certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Men like certainty. They like the Pope to be infallible in faith, and grave doctors to be infallible in morals, so as to have certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observes that people prefer clear, certain authorities; this desire shapes religious expectations and institutional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church teaching vs divine inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church teaches, and God inspires, both infallibly. The work of the Church is of use only as a preparation for grace or condemnation. What it does is enough for condemnation, not for inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes the Church's authoritative teaching (sufficient for moral/legal condemnation) from direct divine inspiration (which is of a different order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of external influence on papal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every time the Jesuits may impose upon the Pope, they will make all Christendom perjured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that powerful advisors (here Jesuits) imposing on the Pope can corrupt wider Christendom; emphasizes vulnerability of a single human office to external manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for genuine salvation/doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Sinners purified without penitence; the righteous justified without love; all Christians without the grace of Jesus Christ; God without power over the will of men; a predestination without mystery; a redemption without certitude!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts core doctrinal necessities (penitence, love, grace, divine agency, mystery, certitude) and criticizes theological positions that omit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worthy ordination required
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one is made a priest, who wants to be so, as under Jeroboam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes lax discipline in making clergy; implies ordination should require worthiness, not merely desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy as guardian of doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The true pastors of the Church, who are the true guardians of the Divine Word, have preserved it unchangeably against the efforts of those who have attempted to destroy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer from individual corruptions (monks, casuists) that God has abandoned the Church; the hierarchical body preserves doctrine against isolated abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Church doctrine from Jesuit doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Heretics, who take advantage of the doctrine of the Jesuits, must be made to know that it is not that of the Church [_the doctrine of the Church_], and that our divisions do not separate us from the altar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When doctrines are misused by sectarians, clarify they are not official Church doctrine; doctrinal disputes or divisions do not necessarily sever sacramental communion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of uniformity and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity without diversity is useless to others; diversity without uniformity is ruinous for us. The one is harmful outwardly; the other inwardly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for a balance: absolute uniformity and complete diversity are each problematic in different ways; a mixed approach is necessary for ecclesial health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion by truth vs critique of ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: By showing the truth, we cause it to be believed; but by showing the injustice of ministers, we do not correct it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To effect belief or reform, present truth rather than merely exposing officials' injustice; critique alone often fails to correct wrongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption of law by corrupt ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who love the Church lament to see the corruption of morals; but laws at least exist. But these corrupt the laws. The model is damaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When those charged with upholding law become corrupt, they damage both law and exemplar standards for the faithful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious conviction can justify evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as when they do it from religious conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning that religiously motivated wrongdoing is especially dangerous because perpetrators believe themselves justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention vs outward act in obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: The servant knoweth not what his lord doeth, for the master tells him only the act and not the intention... And this is why he often obeys slavishly, and defeats the intention. But Jesus Christ has told us the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the moral importance of discerning intentions/objectives behind actions; slavish obedience to acts without understanding intention can subvert true ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not institutionalize exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the men of old given absolution before penance? Do this as exceptional. But of the exception you make a rule without exception, so that you do not even want the rule to be exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against converting exceptional dispensations into general practice; exceptions should remain exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: God judges inwardly; Church judges outwardly
rubrics_metrics.description: God regards only the inward; the Church judges only by the outward. God absolves as soon as He sees penitence in the heart; the Church when she sees it in works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the distinction of spheres: divine judgment of interior disposition versus ecclesiastical concern for external signs; consequently the Church may tolerate disguised hypocrites while God alone sees the heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty vs probability; truth as sole certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: But is it probable that probability gives assurance? Difference between rest and security of conscience. Nothing gives certainty but truth; nothing gives rest but the sincere search for truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects reliance on mere probability for moral assurance; true certainty comes from truth and earnest pursuit of it; distinguishes superficial 'rest' from secure conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose good guides to avoid compounded error
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole society itself of their casuists cannot give assurance to a conscience in error, and that is why it is important to choose good guides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following erroneous teachers magnifies culpability; selecting trustworthy spiritual guides is essential to avoid being led into error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain lust, not scruples
rubrics_metrics.description: They allow lust to act, and check scruples; whereas they should do the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques moral systems that relax passions while suppressing conscientious scruples; argues priorities should be reversed—limit vice rather than conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punish abuse of truth as you would falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: They have some true principles; but they misuse them. Now, the abuse of truth ought to be as much punished as the introduction of falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misapplying correct principles is as dangerous as propagating false doctrines and should be treated similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of probability undermines holiness when based on human authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If they do not renounce their doctrine of probability, their good maxims are as little holy as the bad, for they are founded on human authority; and thus, if they are more just, they will be more reasonable, but not more holy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moral maxims rest on human authority (probability) rather than divine truth, their justice does not ensure holiness; a call to renounce such doctrinal foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity test: compare loves
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us see if we seek God sincerely, by comparison of the things which we love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test for spiritual sincerity: examine and compare the relative loves/attachments in one's life to assess true seeking of God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrition must seek sacrament to remit sins
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not absolution only which remits sins by the sacrament of penance, but contrition, which is not real if it does not seek the sacrament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True contrition requires seeking the sacrament (penitential rite) to be effective in remission; inward sorrow alone is insufficient if it does not pursue sacramental reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political leaders' confession as public image
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to kings and princes to be considered pious; and therefore they must confess themselves to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the political utility for rulers to appear pious by performing public religious acts (e.g., confession), implying pastoral role for clergy in shaping rulers' reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret Scripture from Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: He who will give the meaning of Scripture, and does not take it from Scripture, is an enemy of Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hermeneutical principle: authoritative interpretation must be grounded in Scripture itself rather than external imposition; otherwise the interpreter opposes Scripture.
